prompt.context: Our client, Accountware, is a software company that makes accounting software for public companies. After several strong years, Accountware is looking to make an acquisition. The CEO has narrowed the list of potential targets down to 3 companies: BankWeb, HospitalAccount, and Retail Inventory. Accountware has hired our firm to determine which target it should pursue.
prompt.question: Which of the three acquisition targets — BankWeb, HospitalAccount, or Retail Inventory — should Accountware pursue, and at what price?

clarifying_info.q: What are Accountware's goals for the acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: The CEO wants the acquisition to make both financial and strategic sense.
BankWeb makes websites for banks. HospitalAccount makes accounting software for hospitals. Retail Inventory makes inventory software for clothing stores.

clarifying_info.q: Does Accountware currently work in web development, inventory tracking, or hospital accounting software?
clarifying_info.a: No, Accountware does not work in web development, inventory tracking, or provide accounting software to hospitals.

clarifying_info.q: How much cash does Accountware have?
Are there any regulatory concerns with any of the acquisitions?
clarifying_info.a: There are no regulatory concerns with the acquisition of any of the targets.

exhibits.title: Financial Data for All Three Targets and Accountware
exhibits.shows: Income statement line items (Revenue, COGS, Gross Profit, SG&A, EBITDA) and headcount (Sales people, Software Developers) for BankWeb, HospitalAccount, Retail Inventory, and Accountware

exhibits.title: Recent Comparable Acquisitions
exhibits.shows: A table of recent acquisitions showing company name, market, industry, sales, EBITDA, and acquisition price in $ millions

framework: Analyze each target strategically: industry fit, market size & growth, market share, competitive position, cultural alignment, ownership/willingness to sell
Analyze each target financially: revenue, margins, EBITDA, headcount efficiency (Revenue per salesperson, Revenue per developer)
Identify synergy potential: cost reduction opportunities if Accountware's operational ratios are applied to the target
Combine strategic and financial analysis to select the best target
Estimate acquisition price using comparable transaction multiples from Exhibit 2, applying the relevant industry average and adjusting for the selected target's EBITDA

questions.prompt: From a strategic perspective, discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each target.
questions.guidance:
BankWeb — Pros: industry-leading quality, excellent websites (Forbes award), rapid growth as a company. Cons: flat market growth for regional bank websites; not core to Accountware's accounting software business; culture is start-up vs. Accountware's professional culture.

HospitalAccount — Pros: similar capability set (accounting software), positioning for accelerated growth driven by new healthcare disclosure requirements (market growth accelerated from 2% to 5%), rapidly growing market. Cons: mid-tier quality, only 2% market share.

Retail Inventory — Pros: competes well against larger companies, poised for expansion into other retail/perishable categories. Cons: non-core capabilities (inventory tracking), only 5% market share; PE-owned (purchased 18 months ago — will want to exit at a premium).

Overall strategic winner: HospitalAccount — most aligned with Accountware's core accounting software expertise and benefits from healthcare regulatory tailwind.

questions.prompt: From a financial perspective, which target looks most attractive? (Give Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance:
Surface-level: BankWeb has the highest EBITDA margin (~40%), identical to Accountware's own 30%+ margin profile, making it appear very attractive financially. HospitalAccount has 0% EBITDA margin, which looks weak.

Synergy analysis (HospitalAccount only — interviewer should prompt candidate here): Accountware's Revenue/salesperson = $1,000,000 and Revenue/developer = $500,000. HospitalAccount's Revenue/salesperson = ~$500,000 (35M/70) and Revenue/developer = ~$375,940 (35M/93) — both far below Accountware's ratios, indicating significant overstaffing. If Accountware applies its own staffing ratios, HospitalAccount would need only 35 salespeople (down from 70) and 70 developers (down from 93). This right-sizes SG&A to ~$3.5M and COGS (through developer cost reduction), yielding a revised EBITDA of ~$10.5M (30% margin).

No synergies expected for BankWeb or Retail Inventory per the case.

Conclusion: After synergies, HospitalAccount's financials become the most strategically and financially attractive.

math.setup: Apply Accountware's Revenue/salesperson ($1M) and Revenue/developer ($500K) ratios to HospitalAccount's $35M revenue to find implied efficient headcount, then recalculate P&L.
steps: Revised SG&A (proportional to Accountware's 10% of revenue) = 10% × $35M = $3,500,000
Revised COGS (proportional to Accountware's 60% of revenue) = 60% × $35M = $21,000,000
math.answer: Post-synergy EBITDA for HospitalAccount = $10.5M (30% margin), up from $0

questions.prompt: Which target should Accountware pursue, and what price should it expect to pay? (Give Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance:
Target selection: HospitalAccount — best combined strategic fit (accounting software expertise, healthcare growth tailwind) and best post-synergy financial profile.

Pricing via Exhibit 2 comparable multiples: Use US accounting software comparables (AccountMan and QuickCounting); ignore Japan Accounting (wrong market), Restaurant Tracker (outlier — too large), and Quick Web (outlier — too small for web dev). Compute EBITDA multiples for the relevant comparables and apply to HospitalAccount's post-synergy EBITDA.

For HospitalAccount, use accounting software multiples (6x EBITDA average); apply to post-synergy EBITDA of $10.5M → implied price ≈ $63M. Accountware has $150M in cash so the purchase is feasible.

math.setup: Calculate EBITDA acquisition multiples for comparable transactions, exclude outliers, average the relevant comps, and apply to HospitalAccount's post-synergy EBITDA of $10.5M.
steps: Accounting software average EBITDA multiple = 6.0x (Japan Accounting excluded — wrong market)
For reference — Inventory software comps (excluding Restaurant Tracker outlier): Clothing Tracking 5.0x, Retail Counter 5.0x → avg 5.0x; Retail Inventory EBITDA $6M × 5.0x = $30M
For reference — Web development comps (excluding Quick Web outlier): Web Fast 12.0x, Web Flash 12.0x → avg 12.0x; BankWeb EBITDA $6M × 12.0x = $72M
math.answer: Expected price for HospitalAccount ≈ $63M (6x post-synergy EBITDA of $10.5M); well within Accountware's $150M cash balance

recommendation: Accountware should acquire HospitalAccount. It is the only target with a core capability set (accounting software) that aligns with Accountware's expertise, and it operates in a rapidly growing market (2% → 5% CAGR) driven by new healthcare disclosure regulations. Post-synergy analysis shows that applying Accountware's operational efficiency ratios eliminates HospitalAccount's current 0% EBITDA margin and yields a 30% margin — identical to Accountware's own profile. The estimated acquisition price of ~$63M is well within Accountware's $150M cash balance.
risks: Cultural integration risk: HospitalAccount has been led by the same founder-CEO since 1995 — retirement or departure could remove the key driver of the business
Small market share (2%) means HospitalAccount is not the dominant player; scaling it will require execution
Healthcare regulatory environment could shift, slowing the disclosure-driven growth tailwind
next_steps: Assess the founder-CEO's willingness to remain post-acquisition and succession plan
Conduct deeper due diligence on HospitalAccount's software quality and development roadmap
Confirm ownership's willingness to sell and negotiate price based on 6x post-synergy EBITDA (~$63M)
Evaluate cultural integration plan given long-tenured professional culture at HospitalAccount vs. Accountware
